evals.prompt: I run product at Tilepath, a field-service scheduling SaaS with about 1,900 paying accounts (HVAC contractors, plumbing franchises, commercial landscaping). We store job records, technician GPS pings and invoice line items, and customers increasingly want all of it in their own systems instead of hitting our REST API with a homegrown scraper. We surveyed our top 120 accounts: none of them run Snowflake, Databricks or BigQuery. Their data people use Athena, DuckDB, and a couple of them have Spark on EMR for ML churn models. Every roadmap review someone re-adds a line item called 'Snowflake sharing (later)' and it never dies. Design the bulk export surface for us and tell me what shape it takes.
evals.expected_output: A design that selects the Parquet file-drop on object storage as the camp, and explicitly strikes the native warehouse share from the plan rather than parking it in a later phase, with a named re-promotion trigger.
expectations: Selects Parquet file-drops on object storage as the camp for Tilepath
Removes the native warehouse/lake share from the plan outright rather than ranking it last or scheduling it as a later phase
Justifies that removal on the grounds that a share requires a share-capable destination on the recipient side, which no Tilepath account has
States a named re-promotion trigger for the native share: target accounts concentrating on one shareable warehouse platform
Names roughly 30-40% of target accounts on a single platform as the concentration threshold that would justify a native share
Flags that the 30-40% concentration threshold is a self-set heuristic, not a vendor-published figure
Does not recommend real-time streaming push as the surface for Tilepath
Rejects streaming push citing its effort/efficiency position or its non-replayability trade-off
Notes that Hive-partitioned Parquet is the shape every consuming engine (Spark, Athena, DuckDB) already reads
Notes the file-drop also serves ML backfills and raw-file use cases a warehouse share cannot
Does not propose routing export downloads through Tilepath's own API servers

evals.prompt: Nimbus Ledger here - subscription billing platform, roughly 4,200 customers. We're shipping a data export product next quarter. The data is a mix: append-only billing events, plus invoice and subscription records that get updated and sometimes hard-deleted when a customer disputes a charge. Two problems. First, our head of marketing already published 'hourly data SLA' on the pricing page last week without asking anyone. Second, our data engineering lead wants to skip batch entirely and go straight to Debezium CDC off our Postgres WAL - he ran Debezium at his last company for three years. What cadence do we actually ship, and what do we put in front of customers?
evals.expected_output: A cadence recommendation starting at scheduled full-dump with named promotion conditions, plus an explicitly labeled freshness posture and a correction of the 'hourly SLA' pricing-page language.
expectations: Names exactly one freshness posture for the product and labels it as one of: fixed cadence, best-effort target, or contractual SLA
Flags that 'hourly SLA' on the pricing page reads as a contractual, penalty-backed commitment distinct from a best-effort hourly target, and must either be backed or corrected
States that leaving the posture unnamed makes the best-effort promise in the customer's mind and the no-promise position in the vendor's own
Recommends scheduled full-dump as the starting cadence rung rather than CDC
Cites a full load every 3 hours as a concrete reference cadence in this feature class
Gives named promotion conditions for leaving full-dump: its bandwidth/compute bill exceeding CDC's build cost, or a customer freshness requirement the dump interval cannot meet
States that adopting CDC commits the design to upsert-by-primary-key deduplication
States that adopting CDC requires explicit delete tombstones
Requires a periodic full-scan reconciliation job under CDC
Names missed deletes - a delete that emits no change event - as the CDC failure mode that leaves phantom rows in customer copies
Acknowledges the lead's existing Debezium experience as a legitimate reason to promote the CDC rung earlier than the cost curve alone would

evals.prompt: Quarrystone (product analytics SaaS, ~700 accounts). We ship each customer's event data to their S3 bucket. Current layout is s3://bucket/customer_id=<uuid>/session_id=<uuid>/hour=<ts>/part-*.json.gz - files average 0.2 MB, one line-delimited JSON event per line, and a large account generates upwards of 500,000 files a month. Customers tell us Athena queries take 40+ seconds on a week of data. Our new staff architect's proposal is one sentence: 'migrate the export to Apache Iceberg.' Before I greenlight that, tell me what the export layout should actually be.
evals.expected_output: A written file-layout and partitioning contract fixing cardinality, depth, format, file sizing, compaction and cataloging, with Iceberg adoption declined absent a named graduation trigger.
expectations: Rejects customer_id and session_id as partition keys on high-cardinality grounds
Caps partition depth at roughly 2-3 levels of low-cardinality keys
Prescribes Hive-style partition paths such as year=2026/month=08/day=30/
States partition keys must be chosen by what the consumer filters on, not by how the internal schema is organized
Specifies a target file size of roughly 256-512 MB
Specifies a target Parquet row-group size of roughly 128-512 MB
Recommends replacing JSON with Parquet, citing roughly up to 2x faster unload and up to 6x smaller output
Prescribes a compaction job with a concrete trigger, such as compacting when a table or partition exceeds 100 files each smaller than 75% of the target file size
Cites the measured small-files penalty of roughly 4x (an Athena query dropping from about 40 seconds to about 10 after compaction)
Requires registering the export schema in a catalog (Glue, Hive Metastore, Iceberg REST or equivalent) rather than letting consumers infer it from files
Declines to adopt Iceberg/Delta/Hudi unless the export needs atomic multi-file commits, time-travel, or in-place schema evolution, naming those as the graduation triggers
States that the layout is a written contract rather than whatever the export job happens to emit

evals.prompt: Ferrolane, logistics/freight-visibility SaaS, ~900 customers on the paid tiers. Architecture review Thursday on our new data export. Current design: the customer calls GET /v1/exports/{id}/download on our Go API, we stream the object out of our single export bucket through the API pods, and each customer gets a long-lived IAM user access key pair we email during onboarding so their pipelines can also list the bucket prefix directly. Access reviews are a quarterly calendar task for the security team. Roughly a third of our customers are on Azure rather than AWS. Poke holes in this before Thursday.
evals.expected_output: A review that rejects byte-proxying and static shared keys, replacing them with signed URLs / scoped temporary credentials, per-recipient credentials and encryption grants, and a TTL-pinned review cadence.
expectations: Rejects routing export downloads through Ferrolane's own API servers, naming the API fleet as both the throughput ceiling and the egress payer
Prescribes short-lived pre-signed URLs or scoped temporary credentials so the recipient reads object storage directly
States that the service's remaining job is authorization plus URL-signing
Rejects the long-lived shared access keys, prescribing per-recipient credentials instead
Names cross-account IAM roles with an ExternalId as the AWS mechanism, in place of distributing key material
Names SAS tokens as the Azure equivalent for the Azure-hosted third of customers
Prescribes one KMS grant per recipient so revoking one customer never touches another

Lays out the isolation ladder in order - dedicated bucket per tenant, shared bucket with prefix isolation, per-recipient access points, broker-minted short-term credentials - and advises climbing it only as tenant count forces
Pins the access-review cadence to the credential TTL/expiry rather than the quarterly calendar process
States that key rotation under CMEK/SSE-KMS must not require re-encrypting historical data
Mentions per-file Parquet encryption as the finer-grained option when one shared bucket serves recipients of differing trust levels

evals.prompt: Slatewave, HR/workforce-analytics SaaS. We're launching a native Snowflake share of each customer's people data. Our Snowflake account is in AWS us-east-1; about 40% of the accounts we'd share with sit in eu-central-1 and another 15% in ap-southeast-2. Leadership's plan is to bundle the share free into all three paid tiers as a differentiator against our two main competitors, who both charge for it. Finance asked me one question I couldn't answer - 'does this cost us anything per customer?' - and I realised I have no idea. Write up the cost and pricing section of the design.
evals.expected_output: A cost-allocation section naming who pays storage, compute and egress per delivery model including the cross-region case, plus a recommendation against free bundling on premium-gating precedent.
expectations: Recommends against bundling the export free, stating that no free-tier precedent exists in this feature class

Cites that every vendor studied gates bulk export behind an enterprise tier, a paid plan, or a usage-priced add-on, naming at least one example such as Stripe's transaction-count subscription, Braze's enterprise contract, or HubSpot's top tier
States that in cross-region native sharing the provider can end up paying egress that scales with consumer query volume
Identifies egress as the decisive line item, citing that cross-region and cross-cloud transfer can reach up to roughly 70% of total data-transfer cost
Attributes the ~70% figure to Snowflake as a vendor-published number and weights it as such
Notes same-region transfer is typically free, making the us-east-1 consumers the cheap case and eu-central-1/ap-southeast-2 the expensive ones
Names Snowflake's Egress Cost Optimizer - replicate once, pay egress on increments - as a mitigation, treating its savings figure as a vendor claim
Separates what Slatewave charges from who pays the underlying infrastructure, treating them as independent decisions
States that under a native share nothing is copied, so there is no storage duplication and the consumer pays only query compute
Requires writing down before launch, per delivery model, who pays storage, compute and egress, explicitly including the cross-region path

evals.prompt: Kestrelbridge - payments operations SaaS, we drop nightly Parquet to about 300 customer buckets. Last Tuesday a backend team renamed merchant_ref to merchant_reference in our core service. It flowed straight through the export job. Wednesday morning we had 31 support tickets: broken Looker dashboards, two customers' dbt runs failing, one customer's fraud model silently scoring on nulls for a day. Our VP Eng's proposed fix is 'we'll list column changes in the monthly release notes from now on.' I need something better than that to take to the exec review. What's the policy?
evals.expected_output: An add-only schema-evolution contract with per-batch validation, catalog-registered versions, the four-part data contract framing, and a real deprecation process replacing release-notes-only notice.
expectations: States an add-only posture: append new nullable columns at the end, never rename, remove, or retype in place
Explains that renames break Parquet consumers outright because column names are the identifiers
Prescribes add-the-new-column-and-deprecate-the-old in place of the merchant_ref rename
Requires consistent column ordering and types across every batch
Ties that consistency requirement to predicate pushdown and by-name column matching in consuming engines
Requires validating each batch's written schema against the documented contract before the delivery counts as successful, so drift raises an alert instead of a customer ticket
Requires registering every schema version in the catalog
Frames the commitment as a four-part data contract covering schema, quality, freshness and availability
Treats the export schema as an API contract whose breaking changes ship silently into customer dashboards rather than into Kestrelbridge's own logs
Rejects release-notes-only notice as sufficient, requiring an announced window, parallel old-and-new columns or paths, and a dated removal
Defers the notice-period and sunset machinery to the API versioning/deprecation policy rather than inventing a parallel process here

evals.prompt: Vantablue, payroll and benefits SaaS, ~2,600 customers. Everything customer-facing exports into one bucket in us-east-1 - simplest thing that worked and it's been fine for two years. Facts on the ground: 41% of our customers are EU-based and the export contains names, national IDs and salary; our tier-2 support team in Manila queries that bucket directly with Athena several times a week to debug failed exports; our largest prospect is an Indian conglomerate whose procurement team keeps asking where the data physically sits; and our legal counsel says we have SCCs signed with every EU customer so we're covered. Tell me what actually needs to change before we scale this.
evals.expected_output: A residency posture that recognises remote access as a transfer, fixes it architecture-first via region pinning, corrects the SCCs-are-enough claim, and treats the Indian localization requirement as a hard blocker.
expectations: States that remote access - the Manila support team querying an EEA customer's export - is itself a regulated cross-border transfer, not merely file copying
Recommends region pinning (EU customer data in EU buckets/shares) as the first and preferred fix
Orders the remedies architecture-first - region pinning, then regionalized CMEK, then pseudonymized replicas - with legal paperwork as the fallback rather than the lead
Explains that regionalized CMEK closes the 'the ciphertext moved but it is encrypted' argument, which regulators do not accept as a substitute for a transfer mechanism
Corrects the counsel's position: SCCs alone are insufficient post-Schrems II and a Transfer Impact Assessment is mandatory on top of them
Cites Meta's €1.2 billion 2023 fine as having been specifically for cross-border transfer failures

Treats the Indian data-localization requirement as a hard blocker rather than a paperwork item, and presents explicit non-availability in that region as a legitimate precedented outcome (Stripe does not offer Data Pipeline in India)
Cites Segment deprecating its EU Data Lakes product rather than retrofitting residency, as evidence that retrofitting can cost the whole product
Requires region selection to be built into the early rollout stages rather than bolted on later
Produces per-route transfer documentation covering legal basis, data classes involved, and whether pseudonymization applies
Names the single global us-east-1 bucket as the anti-pattern that silently commits Vantablue to the SCC/TIA paperwork path for every EU customer

evals.prompt: Pulsegrid, in-app messaging and push platform. Our customers' growth teams want message-delivery, open and click events pushed to them in near real time - they say batch files landing every three hours are useless for the intervention loops they're building, they want it inside a minute. Two of our three design partners want it on their own HTTPS endpoint, the third wants Kinesis. Our platform already emits every one of these as a discrete event on an internal bus, so the plumbing is mostly there. Design this export surface and tell me what we commit to publicly.
evals.expected_output: A streaming-push design that qualifies the rung against its three conditions and makes non-replayability an explicit, loud contractual term, alongside a batch surface for backfill.
expectations: Accepts streaming push only against the three named conditions: genuinely event-shaped data, consumer demand for sub-minute delivery, and consumer acceptance of the durability trade-off
States explicitly that with a non-replayable stream a consumer whose endpoint was down recovers nothing from the provider
Requires the public contract or documentation to state non-replayability as loudly as Braze Currents does
Identifies streaming push as the highest-effort rung and the one that loses every efficiency comparison
Recommends also shipping a file-drop or batch surface for historical backfill, which the stream cannot serve
Notes that Avro, with schema-registry-based evolution, rather than Parquet, is the format used on the streaming rung
Does not promise replay, at-least-once recovery or gap-filling unless a separate durable buffer is explicitly designed for it
Keeps the streaming surface gated behind a paid or enterprise contract rather than self-serve, consistent with the precedent in this feature class
States an explicit freshness posture for the stream, labeled as fixed cadence, best-effort target, or contractual SLA
Mentions entity-count batching (such as splitting files per 5,000 users) as an alternative to time-window batching on this rung

evals.prompt: Orchardline, CRM for manufacturing distributors. Reviewing our data-out plan doc before I sign off. Of our 340 target enterprise accounts, 38% are on Databricks; the rest have no warehouse at all and just want files. The doc has four phases: (1) build an in-house file transfer and sharing service so we own the protocol end to end, (2) partitioned Parquet drops, (3) log-based CDC, (4) EU region pinning plus deciding pricing. Team is two data engineers and a half-time SRE. Success criteria in the doc are 'export NPS above 40' and '25% of enterprise accounts adopted by Q4'. Tear this apart and give me the plan you'd actually run.
evals.expected_output: A restaged rollout leading with Delta Sharing and the file drop, pulling residency and pricing forward, rejecting the in-house build, and replacing the NPS/adoption criteria with the four binary gates.
expectations: Puts the native Databricks Delta Sharing surface first, justified by the 38% concentration
Puts the Parquet-on-object-storage file drop second as the universal fallback serving the warehouse-less majority
Rejects deferring EU region pinning to phase 4, requiring it baked into the first two stages
Rejects deferring the pricing decision, requiring the surface priced as an enterprise tier or add-on from day one
Rejects building the in-house file transfer and sharing service, recommending the destination warehouse's own sharing primitive instead
Cites Fivetran acquiring Census in 2025 despite holding a working reverse-ETL prototype as the build-versus-partner evidence
Gives a named revisit trigger for the build-versus-buy choice: vendor usage pricing crossing the fully-loaded cost of roughly 1-2 data engineers
Makes cadence upgrades such as incremental or CDC conditional on full-dump cost or a customer freshness requirement, rather than a scheduled phase
Replaces the NPS and adoption criteria with the four binary gates: contract completeness, cost allocation named, residency coverage, and premium gating
Treats freshness attainment, consumer-reported schema-break incidents and egress cost per recipient as trends to watch rather than pass/fail thresholds
Notes that the effort ranking favouring the native share assumes the data already sits in a share-capable warehouse or lakehouse, and that getting it there flips the ordering
